why:
Water is a pure compound, so by the law of definite proportions it always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass whatever its source (§1.4.2). Water contains only hydrogen and oxygen, so the two percentages by mass must add to 100. Given hydrogen is 11.1 %, oxygen is \(100 - 11.1 = 88.9\) %, so the blank is 88.9.

The other three fail on the same arithmetic: 18 and 16 are the molar mass of water and the atomic mass of oxygen in \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) and u respectively, not percentages, and 80 would leave \(100 - 80 - 11.1 = 8.9\) % of the mass unaccounted for in a compound that contains no third element.

The law of multiple proportions applies only when the SAME two elements A and B form more than one compound; it then says the masses of B that combine with a fixed mass of A are in a ratio of small whole numbers (§1.4.3).

Check each pair. \(\mathrm{NO}\) and \(\mathrm{NO_2}\): both are compounds of N and O, and per 14 g of nitrogen they carry 16 g and 32 g of oxygen, a ratio of 1 : 2. \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\): both are compounds of C and O, and per 12 g of carbon they carry 16 g and 32 g of oxygen, again 1 : 2. \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\): both are compounds of H and O, and per 2 g of hydrogen they carry 16 g and 32 g of oxygen, again 1 : 2 — this is the chapter's own worked illustration. All three pairs therefore DO demonstrate the law.

\(\mathrm{Na_2S}\) and \(\mathrm{NaF}\) are not two compounds of one element pair at all: the first is a compound of sodium and sulfur, the second of sodium and fluorine. There is no second element held in common, so no mass ratio of the kind the law describes can even be formed, and this is the pair that cannot demonstrate it.

The chapter relates the two scales by \(^\circ\mathrm{F} = \dfrac{9}{5}(^\circ\mathrm{C}) + 32\) (§1.3.2 v). The reading is the same on both scales when the numerical value \(x\) satisfies

\(x = \dfrac{9}{5}x + 32\)

\(x - 1.8x = 32\)

\(-0.8x = 32\)

\(x = -40\)

so the two scales read alike at \(-40^\circ\), and this is the only solution because the equation is linear with a non-zero coefficient.

Substituting the other three confirms they fail: \(+40^\circ\mathrm{C}\) gives \(104\ ^\circ\mathrm{F}\), \(-80^\circ\mathrm{C}\) gives \(-112\ ^\circ\mathrm{F}\), and \(-20^\circ\mathrm{C}\) gives \(-4\ ^\circ\mathrm{F}\); in none of these does the Fahrenheit number match the Celsius number.

Table 1.1 of the chapter lists the seven SI base quantities and their units. Against 'Electric current' it gives the ampere, symbol A, so the ampere is the SI unit asked for.

The other three are units of different quantities, and two of them are not base units at all: the volt is the unit of electric potential difference, the newton is the derived unit of force, and the candela — although it IS one of the seven base units in the same table — is the unit of luminous intensity, not of current.

The quantities compared here are VOLUMES of gases reacting under the same conditions, and they are in the simple whole-number ratio 1 : 3 : 2. That is exactly Gay Lussac's law of gaseous volumes: when gases combine or are produced in a chemical reaction they do so in a simple ratio by volume, provided all gases are at the same temperature and pressure (§1.4.4). The chapter states this law using this very reaction, noting that 1 L of nitrogen with 3 L of hydrogen gives 2 L of ammonia.

The others do not fit. The law of definite proportion is about a compound always containing the same elements in the same proportion BY MASS, not about the volume ratio of a reaction. The law of multiple proportions compares two different compounds of the same two elements, and only one compound is formed here. Reciprocal proportion likewise concerns combining masses, and is not the law this volume relationship illustrates.

Equal numbers of molecules mean equal numbers of moles, since the number of molecules is the number of moles multiplied by Avogadro's constant (§1.8). So compare moles, \(n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}\).

7 g of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) (molar mass \(28\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) is \(7/28 = 0.25\) mol.

2 g of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) (molar mass \(2\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) is \(2/2 = 1.0\) mol.

8 g of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) (molar mass \(32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) is \(8/32 = 0.25\) mol.

20 g of \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) (molar mass \(46\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) is \(20/46 = 0.435\) mol.

1.0 mol is the largest of the four by a clear margin, so 2 g of hydrogen holds the most molecules — about \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) of them, against roughly \(1.5 \times 10^{23}\), \(1.5 \times 10^{23}\) and \(2.6 \times 10^{23}\) for the others. Note the trap: 20 g is much the largest MASS and still gives fewer molecules, because \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) is 23 times heavier per molecule than \(\mathrm{H_2}\).

The molar mass of water is numerically equal to its molecular mass in u (§1.8): \(2 \times 1.0 + 16.0 = 18.0\), so \(18.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\). Rearranging \(n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}\) gives

mass \(= n \times\) molar mass \(= 0.25\ \mathrm{mol} \times 18.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} = 4.5\ \mathrm{g}\).

The other three are the near-misses this calculation invites: 18 is the molar mass itself, i.e. the mass of a full mole rather than of a quarter of one; 0.25 is the number of moles quoted straight back as a mass; and 5.4 does not arise from these numbers at all (\(0.25 \times 18 = 4.5\), not 5.4).

Read the unit carefully — the volume is \(22.4\ \mathrm{cm^3}\), not \(22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}\). Since \(1\ \mathrm{dm^3} = 1000\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) (§1.3.2 iii), \(22.4\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 0.0224\ \mathrm{dm^3}\).

The molar volume of a gas at STP is \(22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}\) (§1.9), so

\(n = \dfrac{0.0224\ \mathrm{dm^3}}{22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Number of molecules \(= n \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{20}\).

\(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) is what you get by mistaking the cubic centimetres for cubic decimetres, which is exactly the trap the question sets; \(22.4 \times 10^{20}\) and \(22.4 \times 10^{23}\) simply carry the volume 22.4 into the answer instead of Avogadro's constant, and neither is a number of molecules that follows from any correct step.

Each sample is 1 g, so the sample with the most atoms is the one with the smallest mass per atom, i.e. the lightest atoms. Compute moles of ATOMS in 1 g using the average atomic masses (Au 197, Na 23, Li 6.94, Cl 35.5), remembering that chlorine is supplied as \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) and so carries two atoms per molecule.

1 g Au: \(1/197 = 5.08 \times 10^{-3}\) mol of atoms, about \(3.06 \times 10^{21}\) atoms.

1 g Na: \(1/23 = 4.35 \times 10^{-2}\) mol of atoms, about \(2.62 \times 10^{22}\) atoms.

1 g Li: \(1/6.94 = 0.144\) mol of atoms, about \(8.68 \times 10^{22}\) atoms.

1 g \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\): \(1/71 = 1.41 \times 10^{-2}\) mol of molecules, so \(2.82 \times 10^{-2}\) mol of atoms, about \(1.70 \times 10^{22}\) atoms.

Lithium gives the largest count, roughly three times the next largest, because it has by far the smallest atomic mass of the four. Doubling for the two atoms in each chlorine molecule is not enough to overtake it, and gold — the heaviest — gives the fewest atoms of all despite being the same 1 g.
